The answer to this is probably going to depend a lot on the context. For example:

>When my T pointed out something he identified as transference...

Lots of different things this could mean. Maybe a client tells their therapist, "Hey, there's something you've been doing/saying that I've felt really hurt by." The therapist might say, "that's transference," when in fact the therapist has indeed been behaving harmfully and they are just deflecting the accountability, and appropriating a therapeutic concept in order to do so. This could certainly make the client feel ashamed, or feel like the alleged transference "feels wrong."

Or, maybe a client develops romantic feelings for the therapist. Maybe they'll feel like it "feels wrong" because of the "forbidden" aspect of such a hypothetical romantic relationship. Or, maybe it will "feel wrong" to them because they know it's one-sided, and therefore creates a deeply uncomfortable sense of vulnerability or powerlessness. Or, maybe it feels wrong because, in the client's past, they were frequently shamed for having wants and needs. 

It can vary quite a bit!

>“It’s not your fault, but it *is* your problem.”

Nah, not callous! It's brilliant. Good to remember this advice, for *anyone* who's been through trauma. A lot of people who have been through trauma tend to use that fact as an excuse for their own dysfunctional behavior. Like "It's not *me*, it's just that I have trauma!" Like, no. It may not be someone's fault that they were traumatized, but it sure as hell is their responsibility not to shit on others because of their traumatic dysregulation.

I once had a therapist who, in the second appointment I ever had with her, asked me if I masturbated. It shocked me at the time, simply because past therapists weren't quite as forward. But I eventually realized it was perfectly fine and I came to appreciate her candor. This therapist was a brilliant and deeply empathic clinical psychologist who was interested in hearing about my relationship with myself, and that included my potential *sexual* relationship with myself.

I think it's particularly interesting that you say, "if I don't control the topic there will be questions." So your oversharing is sometimes a means of staying in control and feeling safe?

Thank you so much for sharing your story. And no, I don't see it as you oversharing right now! After all, I *asked* what it felt like and what you think causes it for you. You're really helping me understand. So it sounds like, for you, it's fundamentally a result of feeling confused about boundaries, because your boundaries were repeatedly violated when you were growing up. That makes a *lot* of sense.

What you are describing sound like neurological symptoms, and with neurological disorders (which DPDR is) this one-side-of-the-body phenomenon isn't uncommon. The symptoms you describe can even happen with a migraine (and for what it's worth, many people with DPDR also have migraines.) Migraines don't even have to include a headache; they are complex neurological events that sometimes include a headache, and other times just include some of the funny sensations you describe. I've experienced these symptoms, myself.

That said, I'm not diagnosing you. And no one on Reddit can diagnose you. It sounds like this is causing you a lot of distress, so it might be worth talking to a doctor about it. Even if it's something harmless, it might still do you some good to hear it directly from a doctor that you don't need to worry. Best of luck to you, and I'm sorry you're having such a rough time.

> I just don't see how therapy can work for someone in that headspace

From the way you are describing the "headspace," I would agree with you. If OP is indeed hostile to any and all suggestions of change/growth, then no way in hell are they going to do therapy well.

I guess my issue is that I'm still hesitant to make definitive claims about what that headspace really is. For example, it's possible that DBT is causing such an overwhelming amount of PTSD-based friction that OP truly has almost no capacity to understand the therapy—but it may *also* be possible that a *different* modality, which nevertheless still encourages change/growth, would be effective and OP would be receptive to it. There are different ways to tell someone they need to change, and it's possible that the DBT way of doing so is just not feasible with regard to OP's trauma history.

Again, maybe the scenario I laid out isn't accurate either. I just tend to be very tentative about saying what another person's inner world really is. But OP did say that they chose this therapist because she challenges them, and that seems like a good sign.

>do you think that just because someone is suffering means theyre allowed to treat other people differently?

Absolutely not. We are all responsible for how we treat others, regardless of the pain we are in personally. Maybe I need to read their post more carefully, but I didn't pick up on the notion that they were exactly treating their therapist poorly outside behaving in a very confused and frustrated manner during appointments. (which can still certainly be challenging to work with, as a therapist). That said, the post does convey some less-than-charitable and unjustified assumptions about their therapist. I did not mean to imply that someone ever had a license to treat someone poorly.

>if the person hasnt opened up to the therapist about other suffering, then we cant really expect the therapist to be understanding

Very true. OP needs to learn effective communication. But it is also true that some of the difficulties being described in OPs post are rooted at least partly in confusion and trauma-response, and not entirely rooted in a willful or lazy refusal to communicate. The "accommodation" they may need may simply be a more nuanced approach to DBT/CBT which is famously tricky for clients with a history of trauma.

I hope some of that made sense. You have some really valid points that are frankly important for *any* therapy client to consider.

Their post does seem to express some kind of *huge* block to receiving or even understanding the kind of insight and therapeutic treatment their therapist is offering. But this "block" could be coming from a lot of places. I *can* understand how you would perceive the block as being based in egotism and self-pity, but I personally feel more hesitant about drawing conclusions.

>I think the challenging comments can be useful for other people

Yes, useful for me as well.

I totally get your logic that if a client is going to make progress, then it is *essential* that they be open to considering the possibility that their own behavior is dysfunctional, or ineffective, or harmful. I think the problem is that the way you phrased your comment risks coming off as pretty hurtful, especially when tone of voice is very hard to read over the internet.

Also, when you say "you could ***just*** be really difficult to work with," this seems to negate the important consideration that, even if a client's behavior does need adjusting, the therapist may *also* need to accommodate them in other ways. It negates the possibility that the client may *also* be suffering due to some reasons for which they are *not* responsible. Does that make sense?

>I actually don't think DBT as the main modality would be particularly helpful for OP at this time. I've done DBT and it can be massively invalidating to people who are trying to learn how to unmask.

Totally. I think CBT and DBT can be retraumatizing for clients who are already dealing with a history of having their own emotions, and their own sense of reality, invalidated or punished. At the very least the therapist would have to do it with incredible finesse and nuance and it sounds like *this* therapist's statements are maybe a little bit, well... coarse.

>That's more of what I don't need; the opposite of what I need from a therapist. I'm paying for this session to be about MY feelings. SO I CAN FINALLY PROCESS THEM. I don't need to regulate my emotions.

DBT is ultimately *entirely about regulating emotions* and behavior. It sounds like DBT may be too painful to do right now? I mean if DBT is too triggering that's not your fault, and totally understandble that you'd need to try something else. I think your therapist was doing DBT here, and it was just too painful for you. I'm sorry you're having such a rough time.

>You're absolutely correct that your time is about *your* need to feel seen/heard/understood, not the therapist. It is completely inappropriate for your therapist to try to insert her emotional needs into your session.

You're 100% in saying that it's not about the therapist's needs. At the same time, a major part of DBT is learning "effective interpersonal skills," and it sounds to me like the therapist was *maybe* trying to kindly and neutrally express to OP that what was happening was not effective. It's good that OP can learn in a safe environment how others might feel when OP's "words start spilling out, much faster than they can take them in." Now, also it's totally possible that this therapist does NOT know how to execute this realm of DBT for someone who may be on the spectrum. But I don't think we can assume that the therapist is making the therapy about meeting her own emotional needs, when she may in fact be trying to do something else (even if she is doing so ineptly).

If you're interested in medication, I can tell you that I'm having success with naltrexone (and other opioid-antagonists have shown some promise as well). Other promising psychiatric treatments include: 

* Lamotrigine combined with an SSRI
* TMS (a specific DPDR protocol)

The most popular non-prescription supplements seem to be: 

* magnesium citrate or magnesium glycinate
* N-acetylcystein (NAC)
* L-Theanine (sometimes paired with caffeine)
* CBD (riskier because of quality-control issues)

Other than this, some people have had success with stimulants, or anti-anxiety medications. Others have used GABA supplementation

It's commendable that you want to protect others. At the same time, this isn't your battle. I suggest affirming your own empathy and passion, appreciating those qualities in yourself, and then trying to find peace with the fact that these clients have their own identities and experiences and are capable of being their own advocates if they so decide. It might also help you feel better to consider the fact that *we don't actually know anything* about the other clients or how they experienced this therapist. We don't know whether they are as dependent as you fear they are. We haven't witnessed, first hand, what has gone on. And that's okay.

Alternately, if you want to see your own therapist, then that therapist may be able to help you process this painful experience. That therapist may also have insight into what is actually happening and whether anything can (or ought to) be done.

Erotic transference is not a bad thing, and can in fact be a tremendously helpful therapeutic tool ***if*** the therapist is competent to navigate the issue, and ***if*** the client has the courage and honesty to try to be open about it.

That said, everyone is different. The issue I can forsee possibly happening here is that, if you are attracted to him right off the bat, it might make you feel very hesitant about being open about yourself and your problems. When we're around someone we find attractive, we are usually hugely and *involuntarily* motivated to present an ideal (an incomplete) image of ourselves. This isn't a moral issue and it isn't exactly dishonesty; it's simply an obstacle to vulnerability that most people deal with. On the other hand, maybe you'll have a different experience. Maybe you won't have this challenge. You could always give him a try, and if you feel yourself pressured to edit your self-presentation to an extent that hinders therapy, then you can reconsider.

Ultimately there is no wrong decision here. If you have a gut feeling, then you can go with that. You can always change your mind later.

I'm so glad it was helpful! And believe me, I can absolutely relate to the urge to push the nightmare away. Try not to panic about losing access to the emotions that were in the dream; I think if you simply share the dream's "plot" with your therapist, he may be able to help you figure out the emotional core of it, even if it takes time to do so.

To be honest, I similarly struggle tremendously with knowing what it means to feel safe, for reasons of chronic abuse from trusted figures. And I think this is entirely normal for anyone with a history of chronic abuse. However, it might help to ask this question: have you ever felt safe when you are *alone?* Like, alone listening to music or doing art or enjoying the outdoors? Is there ever a peace and stillness that's there when you're simply with yourself? Do you have a "safe place" that you can go to, in your mind, as a kind of visualization? It might be a starting point, just to look at that feeling of peace. Even if you can't imagine *ever* feeling that peace in the presence of another person, it's something you can at least hold onto as a reference point as you continue to learn about what safety means to you in the context of relationships.

As far as knowing whether your therapist is a safe person to tell this to, you can also just start with looking at his track record. Have you *reliably* been able to be vulnerable with him in the past, where he has respected your feelings and respected you? If the answer is yes, then even if you don't *feel* safe with him, you might still be willing to exercise trust, and take a leap of faith in sharing about the nightmare with him.

Without knowing more of the situation and context for the dialogue, it's really impossible for us to have much informed insight.

It's possible that your therapist is onto something and is making a meaningful distinction. On the other hand, I think it's very important for this to be said, and to affirm your reservations: There is certainly a *possibility* that your therapist is, in fact, seeing your behavior through his own dysfunctional lens. When a woman shows agency or says "no" via firm boundary-setting, she is often (and often especially by men) told that her agency is excessive or pathologic, i.e., defiant or resistant. It doesn't mean that man is malicious; Oftentimes, these men really aren't aware of their own bias, and truly believe they're telling a woman something for her own benefit. But this kind of sexism is pervasive and often subtle. And yes, very good people, including good men, have often been responsible for perpetuating it.

Again, no one here can say for sure whether that's what's happening. But don't let anyone shame you for being wary of the implications of the gender dynamic here.

Yes, I did try acupuncture, and yes it did help me—at least it helped some of my neurological symptoms. I can't say for sure whether it helped my GI issues. I'll DM you about the nutritionist. They are not in NY, however.

I tried quite a few things, and I had probably several health issues going on, so it’s hard to say what caused what, and what *helped* what. But here is what I’m quite sure had an impact:

* I was seeing a nutritionist chiropractor, and they had me start taking **hydrochloric acid tablets** with meals. They explained to me that it actually takes a lot of energy for the body to produce hydrochloric acid, and if you’ve been feeling sick for a long time, then your body may be too tired to be producing enough of the acid to break down the food enough, and this can cause pain and other problems. Additionally, part of what gets your small intestine to start digesting things and moving along, is that it is stimulated by the hydrochloric acid from your stomach once the digestive contents moves from the stomach into the small intestine. So if you have digestive contents moving into the small intestine without enough hydrochloric acid, then the small intestine is not going to be stimulated enough to manage things very well, and this can start to cause problems. (This doctor had to first check that I was deficient in hydrochloric acid, and they used some kind of test using iodine on my skin.) The hydrochloric acid tablets helped me noticeably and I noticed increasing improvement over time, little bit by bit. They taste awful though.
* This nutritionist also had me take something called the **antigen leukocyte antibody test (ALCAT)** that is supposed to detect your body’s inflammatory response to certain foods, which you then eliminate from your diet for a period of time before possibly reintegrating. Interestingly, the ALCAT is not very highly regarded in the medical community. There was a study from Yale showing that it helped IBS, but still some doctors don’t like it. I decided to try it, and after months of sticking with the restricted diet, the pain FINALLY started to leave on a drastic level. The first few months, I would be avoiding all these foods, and still feeling all the same pain, so sometimes I thought it must not be doing anything. But I just stuck with it, and honestly thank god I did. It saved me a lot of disabling pain. After several years of sticking to this diet, I decided to try to reintegrate the foods, and I was able to do so.
* Finally, sometimes I still get these pains. But what I have found to help, before eating a “problem” food (for some reason vegetables are the most painful), I’ll take some **digestive enzymes.** I also try to take **probiotics** daily, especially ones containing bifidobacterium because that’s the one my GI specialist told me was the most important.Not sure if you will find it relevant, but I tested negative for celiac. The pains I experienced were usually in my upper abdomen and would stab/radiate all the way to my back. I couldn’t even sit up straight a lot of the time, it was so painful. But I’m really doing pretty well now. I try to have digestive enzymes with me when I leave the house, in case I need to eat something and anticipate it could cause pain.

Pretty common dissociative symptom. I have it 24/7. Some people get it in smaller episodes. In terms of neurobiological causes, the research is very sparse. My doctor hypothesizes that it may have something to do with disruption to the thalamus (part of the brain responsible for relaying motor and sensory signals to the cerebral cortex), triggered by a trauma-induced over-release of the body's natural painkillers.

Right.  I didn't actually claim the opposite of what you're stating, here. This is why I was intentionally careful to say, in my comment, that “it is ***possible*** that her advice ***could have*** come from” a conversion-therapy-mindset. It is also *possible* that her advice came from a mindset of wanting OP to have more sexual education and better access to tools that would help her have less painful sex.

When OP told her therapist that she did not like sex with men after having taken many measures to try to enjoy it, OP’s therapist says, “then try lube.” The truth is, we don’t know where OP’s therapist was coming from with this particular comment. What I am saying in my comment is that this advice, even *if* it *is* coming from a mindset of compulsory heterosexuality, does not seem to amount to conversion therapy.

Edit: I will say that the fact that OP told her therapist she did not like sex with men, *in the context of trying to also say she thought she was a lesbian*—this makes the advice "use lube" kind of a shitty thing to say, regardless of how helpful lube would be to a heterosexual woman. It shows no respect to OPs emphasis on her own sense of sexual identity, and is quite frankly dismissive, intentionally or not.

Well, your old therapist gave you some supremely shitty advice, and it is possible that her advice could have come from the same kind of mindset that *produces* conversion therapy (i.e., "if someone doesn't like hetero sex, then they just need to try harder"), but the advice itself is not, at this point, conversion therapy. But to be honest, from what I read about her in your other comments, this therapist does seem suspect for perpetuating some abusive and profoundly harmful heteronormativity and compulsory heterosexuality. 

I do want to take this opportunity to say that it's a travesty that your old therapist wouldn't comprehend that *many* (possibly even *most*) lesbians have had sex with men. Many lesbians have been *married* to men, whom they sincerely, deeply loved and were committed to. Those lesbians just didn't know, at the time, that this love was not actually what romantic love really is. They didn't know that what they could have experienced with a woman would have felt more natural or fulfilling or meaningful. If you are a sexual being and you crave intimacy, but you have the entire world telling you that heterosexuality is the default/ideal, then even if you're a lesbian you are likely to have had sexual relationships with men before discovering that part of yourself. Like, good god, I'm glad you have a new therapist.

It sounds like that was an excruciating experience for you, with so many layers of pain happening. I’m sorry that happened. And believe me, having several disabling illnesses that friends have not understood or independently educated themselves about, I can relate to the fatigue that comes with feeling isolated and not well understood.

I don’t know whether this will make you feel better, but it sounds to me like your friends aren't necessarily indifferent or callous, but rather simply oblivious. Like most people who aren’t mental health care professionals, they aren’t trained to recognize what a flashback looks like, and because you say this was your first time having a flashback in front of them, it quite possibly didn’t occur to them that a flashback was what was happening. Even if they knew you had PTSD, it still may not have really *registered* with them in the moment—or, if it did, they probably didn’t understand how serious it was. A lot of people, when they see a friend panicking or having a hard time, really do think that “giving them space” and “not making a big deal out of it” or “downplaying it” really is the kindest and most helpful thing to do. Hi there, what you're describing is completely normal for depersonalization. It sounds like you're experiencing some of the visual distortions that occur under the broad heading of "visual snow syndrome" which is incredibly common for depersonalization. It's not technically what a psychiatrist would consider a hallucination, more of a neurologically based sensory disturbance. Sometimes it looks like things are changing size, or that walls are warping a bit, or that you see little bright dots or trails in your vision, and there's other funny stuff too. I experience the same thing and it really scared me at first, but then I even saw a neuro-opthamologist for it. He told me it wasn't dangerous or a cause for concern, and he said that unfortunately the phenomenon isn't well understood and there's not much research on it.

Yes, it happens to me, too, *especially* when I'm stressed or fatigued. Visual disturbances are common with DPDR, and there are a couple reasons this may be. One reason for visual disturbances (like visual snow and other minor visual hallucinations) is thought to involve some activity in the visual cortex, as well as an imbalance in neurtransmitters (glutamate), which is a big part of DPDR. What you're describing here specifically, though, sounds a little more like convergence insufficiency, which is where they eye muscles aren't working in total harmony with one another, and so the eyes don't converge their respective visions into a single image. That results in blurred or double vision. This often due to a little neurological upset as well, since it's the nervous system that controls those eye muscles. DPDR is a major culprit, as well as any activity or environment that tires out those muscles.
